newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lamfalussy - monetary strategies can be combined.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy - monetary strategies can be combined.

text.p: European Monetary Institute President Alexandre Lamfalussy on Wednesday sought to downplay a debate over which monetary strategy should be adopted for the single European currency, saying the systems could be combined.

Lamfalussy said the systems most widely discussed -- monetary targeting favoured by the Bundesbank and directly targeting inflation favoured by the Bank of England -- were more similar than different and that both seek price stability.

The German central bank has been pushing for the future European Central Bank to adopt a monetary strategy, which reviews money supply to monitor inflation, while the British central bank has pushed for its inflation system to be adopted.

"It should be pointed out that similarities between the behaviour of central banks which pursue these two strategies seem to be greater than the differences, in general, and that the combination of these strategies might not be impossible," Lamfalussy said in the text of a speech.
An advance text of the speech by Lamfalussy to a banking group in Duesseldorf was made available under embargo.

Lamfalussy said central banks applying inflation targeting include monetary aggregates among their indicators while the Bundesbank, which applies monetary targeting, does not react to movements in monetary aggregrates "in a mechanical way."

The choice of which system to use is left open in the Maastricht Treaty, which provides the guidelines to implement currency union in January 1999. The decision must be finalised shortly before the start of the currency union.

Lamfalussy said research shows the monetary targeting system could be feasible because money demand at the level of the European Union is fairly stable and M3 money supply, a general measure of funds in circulation, is controllable.

He also said directly targeting inflation "could be particularly useful" if money demand was unstable due to financial innovations in the run-up to currency union or after the new currency, to be called the Euro, is introduced.
Lamfalussy said convergence among central banks in the use of monetary policy instruments was "well under way," noting the use of open market operations and security repurchase funds.

In addition, Lamfalussy said "a certain convergence" was evident in required reserves and standing facilities and that there was "broad consensus on the main lines of the operational framework of the future single monetary policy".
